notes.meaning: John writes this letter to his dear friend Gaius, referring to himself as the elder because of his age and spiritual leadership. He expresses deep Christian love for Gaius based on the truth of the gospel. Gaius was a common name at the time, and this particular believer was treasured for his genuine faith.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the letter was written not by John the apostle, but by another early Christian leader known as John the presbyter.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition generally views Gaius as a devoted layman with personal financial means rather than an ordained church official.

notes.meaning: John prays that Gaius will enjoy good physical health and success in his daily life, matching the spiritual health of his soul. A healthy soul is one that is forgiven, rooted in God's word, and growing in love. Believers may rightly ask God for bodily strength so they can continue to serve Him well.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some popular teachers treat this greeting as a divine promise guaranteeing physical health and financial wealth to every faithful Christian.

notes.meaning: Traveling Christian teachers returned to John with wonderful news about Gaius. They reported that Gaius held firmly to true doctrine and lived it out every day. Hearing about a friend's steady life of faith brought great gladness to the apostle's heart.

Nothing brings a devoted pastor or spiritual father greater happiness than knowing his spiritual children are living by God's truth. Walking in truth means far more than just knowing right facts; it means putting that faith into practice with sincerity and love.

Gaius proved his faithful character by opening his home to traveling Christian workers, even though they were complete strangers to him. In the ancient world, visiting preachers depended on local believers for food and a safe place to sleep. Caring for fellow believers in practical ways is a true sign of Christian love.

These traveling workers publicly told John's home church about the loving kindness Gaius had shown them. John encourages Gaius to keep helping them by providing supplies, money, and food for the next stage of their travels. Sending servants of Christ on their journey with such care honors God.

These missionaries set out purely to make the name of Jesus Christ known to the world. They deliberately refused to accept money or supplies from the non-believers they were trying to reach. By depending only on Christians, they kept their motives clear and protected the reputation of the gospel.

Since traveling preachers took nothing from outsiders, the church had a duty to welcome them and support their needs. When believers provide shelter, food, or funds to gospel workers, they share in their labor. Helping those who preach makes every giver an active partner in spreading God's truth.

John had sent a previous letter to the local church, but a proud leader named Diotrephes refused to listen. Diotrephes loved to put himself first and wanted total control over the congregation. His pride led him to reject the guidance of the apostle and turn away his messengers.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest Diotrephes was defending the independence of his local congregation against outside authority rather than acting purely out of personal arrogance.

notes.meaning: Diotrephes spread malicious, empty gossip against John and refused to show hospitality to the visiting teachers. Even worse, he stopped others in the church from helping them and kicked out anyone who dared to show kindness. John warned that when he arrived in person, he would publicly confront this abusive behavior.

John urges Gaius not to imitate the proud, selfish conduct of Diotrephes, but to follow what is good. A person's daily actions show what kind of relationship they have with God. Doing good is the fruit of belonging to God, while persisting in cruel and unloving actions shows that someone does not truly know Him.

In direct contrast to Diotrephes, Demetrius is presented as a faithful Christian praised by everyone who knew him. His life matched the teachings of the gospel, so the truth itself confirmed his good character. John and his companions gave him their full backing, likely commending him as the bearer of this letter.

John had many other important things to tell Gaius, but he did not want to write them out with pen and ink. In those days, letters were written on sheets with reed pens, which took time and effort. John decided that the sensitive matters facing their church were best handled in person.

John hoped to visit Gaius very soon so they could talk directly with one another. He closes his letter by wishing Gaius God's peace and sending warm greetings from the local believers. He asks Gaius to personally greet each of their Christian friends by name.
